clue.text: According to Spooner, Apostolic Palace is somewhere to visit

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so his name tells you to swap initial sounds

blocks.note: a palace is a royal court, and apostolic can mean belonging to Saint Paul the apostle; swap the C and P sounds

explanation.surface: A tourist tip: the Pope's residence in Vatican City is worth a visit.
explanation.walkthrough: COURT OF PAUL becomes PORT OF CALL when the initial C and P sounds trade places. 'Apostolic' points at Paul, one of the apostles, rather than the Pope.
explanation.definitionFit: A port of call is literally a harbour where a ship stops, and figuratively any stop made during a trip.

clue.text: I’m not responding to that amorous advance

blocks.note: first meaning: what a quiz contestant says when declining to answer
second meaning: a romantic approach, as in 'make a ___ at someone'

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence rebuffing a romantic approach, but it splits into two separate meanings of one four-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying the word declines a question in a quiz, and the same word names a flirtatious move made towards someone.

clue.text: Lightly cooked and ate cheesy dish

blocks.note: meat cooked only briefly is rare
bit as the past tense of bite, taking food into the mouth

explanation.surface: Someone eats a quick, lightly cooked cheese dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ate' is loosely matched with BIT, the past tense of bite; read together the first words sound like a description of the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh rarebit is melted cheese sauce on toast, a classic British savoury snack.

clue.text: Collection of backscratchers?

blocks.note: surface reading: a set of long-handled tools for scratching an itchy back
setter's reading: a group of people who do each other favours, 'you scratch my back and I'll scratch yours'

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: backscratchers here are people trading favours, not gadgets. The phrase describes former pupils of the same elite schools helping each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Mutual favour-trading among former schoolmates from privileged backgrounds is exactly the informal system the phrase describes.

clue.text: Box prisoner, hooking a right

indicators.note: to hook something is to catch and hold it, so one piece takes others inside it

blocks.note: con is short for convict
taken as written
RT is a standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A boxing picture: a prisoner throws a right hook in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a verb about fighting, and 'hooking a right' continues the boxing image, but Box is the noun definition and hooking means holding.
explanation.definitionFit: A carton is a cardboard container, a kind of box for packing goods such as milk or eggs.

clue.text: Recalled the Spanish court hearings regularly used stands

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters go back the way they came
at regular intervals, so take every second letter

blocks.note: el is the Spanish for the
CT is the abbreviation for court
the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Someone recalls Spanish court hearings that regularly used stands.
explanation.walkthrough: Court here is just its abbreviation, not part of the source for alternate letters. Reversal of EL gives LE.
explanation.definitionFit: A lectern is a sloping desk on a stand for reading or speaking, so lecterns are reading stands.

clue.text: Substitute sewer essentially with external drain

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so take the central letter
something external goes around the outside, so it wraps the other piece

blocks.note: to sap is to drain energy
the middle letter of a five-letter word

explanation.surface: A plumbing job: replace the inside of a sewer with an outside drain.
explanation.walkthrough: The plumbing picture of sewers and drains is the misdirection; drain is a verb meaning weaken.
explanation.definitionFit: To substitute one thing for another is to exchange them, a verb sense matching trade or switch.

clue.text: Receive tax bringing in European container of alcohol

indicators.note: to bring something in is to admit it inside, so a letter goes between the pieces

blocks.note: to win a prize is to receive it
E is the abbreviation for European
VAT is value added tax, the UK sales tax

explanation.surface: A tax receipt from importing a European cask of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion goes between the two words of the charade rather than inside one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A vat is a large tank, and one used in winemaking holds fermenting grape juice, which is alcohol.

clue.text: Kitchen employee cooked perch fast, stuffed with something unknown

indicators.note: cooking turns raw ingredients into a changed dish, so the letters are rearranged
a stuffed dish has a filling packed inside it, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
in algebra x, y and z stand for unknown quantities

explanation.surface: A cook prepares perch quickly, stuffing the fish with a mystery filling.
explanation.walkthrough: Perch is the fish, but here just letters; fast is not a speed but part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastry chef works in a restaurant kitchen making cakes, desserts and baked goods.

clue.text: Traveller on street is one walking

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing placed on another comes after it, so the first-named piece goes second

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
a rider travels on horseback or by bike

explanation.surface: A traveller on foot along a street is someone walking.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, 'on' puts the traveller after the street.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone striding takes long confident steps, so a person walking that way is described by this noun.

clue.text: Firmly joins me tucking into French bread

indicators.note: to tuck into food is to eat it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: bread is slang for money, and cents are the small coins of the euro used in France
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone eating a baguette, tucking in hungrily.
explanation.walkthrough: French bread looks like a baguette but is slang: bread means money.
explanation.definitionFit: To cement two things is to bond them solidly with mortar or adhesive, hence to unite them firmly.

clue.text: Suspect noisy alarm is ringing about examination in chemistry

indicators.note: something suspect is dubious and not to be taken at face value, so rearrange
to ring something is to encircle it

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
c is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A dubious fire alarm going off noisily during a chemistry exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing' fits the alarm in the surface, but it is the container signal; 'about' is the single letter C.
explanation.definitionFit: Microanalysis is chemical analysis of very small quantities of a substance, a specialised laboratory examination.

clue.text: Reveal person’s confidential details doctor pens down along with insurance information

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: sawbones, shortened to bones, is old slang for a doctor
feeling down is feeling low
insurance protection is called cover

explanation.surface: A doctor writes down a patient's insurance details and leaks them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' looks like writing, but here it means encloses. Bones is also the nickname of the ship's doctor in Star Trek.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means exposing someone's secret identity or concealed role, revealing hidden private facts about them.

clue.text: Companies stocking material for dressing arms

indicators.note: a shop stocking goods holds them inside

blocks.note: a flock is a company of birds or sheep
lint is soft fabric used to dress wounds

explanation.surface: Firms that supply cloth for bandaging injured arms.
explanation.walkthrough: Arms looks like limbs needing a dressing; it means weapons. 'For' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A flintlock is an old type of gun fired by a flint striking steel, so flintlocks are weapons.

clue.text: Concealed camping location near the Hollywood Sign?

blocks.note: the Hollywood Sign overlooks Los Angeles, abbreviated LA
a tent is where a camper sleeps

explanation.surface: A hidden campsite in the hills by the famous Hollywood letters.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the wordplay is a little loose: a tent pitched in Los Angeles is an LA tent.
explanation.definitionFit: Latent means present but not yet visible or developed, hidden beneath the surface.

clue.text: Lacking in lyrical quality, novel put on ice

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new form

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A dull, prosaic novel gets shelved, its publication put on hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the book being shelved, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing without the music or imagination of verse is called prosaic, the opposite of poetic.

clue.text: Stars rolled up before party for polymath

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: Leo is a constellation, a group of stars
a ball that rolled ran along the ground
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Film stars arrive rolled up in limos before a party.
explanation.walkthrough: Leonardo da Vinci, painter, engineer and inventor, is the archetypal Renaissance polymath.
explanation.definitionFit: A polymath is someone expert in many fields; da Vinci excelled in art, anatomy, engineering and science.

clue.text: Dull bores indoors ignored now and then – never mind

indicators.note: skipping something at intervals drops every other letter
to bore is to drill into, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters remain
a matte finish is dull, not shiny

explanation.surface: Dull people stuck inside are ignored now and then, but never mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bores' looks like dull people; it is the verb drilling in. Alternate letters of the indoors word are thrown away.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dismissive idioms telling someone a thing is unimportant and can be forgotten.

clue.text: After rising before noon, fabulous being cycling somewhere in London

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising reads from bottom to top
going round in a cycle moves the last letter to the front

blocks.note: am, ante meridiem, means before noon
a fairy is a creature of fable

explanation.surface: A mythical creature gets up in the morning and rides a bike around a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' sets the order: the rising piece comes first. Mayfair is an expensive district of central London.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayfair is a wealthy district of the West End, so it is one particular place in the capital.

clue.text: Fabricated some of account, ruefully

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters sit within it

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Someone sheepishly admits part of their story was made up.
explanation.walkthrough: accoUNT RUEfully contains the answer, spanning the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: A fabricated story is invented, so it is false rather than factual.

clue.text: Clubs abandoning team ceremony for new version

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave behind, so a letter drops away

blocks.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
a crew is a team, as in rowing
a rite is a ritual ceremony

explanation.surface: Clubs that give up a team ritual and start afresh.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs is just the letter C, dropped from the start of the team word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rewrite is a revised text, a fresh draft that replaces the earlier one.

clue.text: Leaders in concert hall said to be concerning singers

indicators.note: leaders go first, so take the opening letters

blocks.note: the initials of the two words
oral means spoken

explanation.surface: Gossip about singers from the bosses at a concert venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said to be' sounds like a sound-alike signal, but said is simply the spoken meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Choral describes anything relating to a choir, a group of vocal performers.

clue.text: Deposit coppers and assert what’s required

blocks.note: to deposit something is to set or lay it down
coppers are police officers, informally the law

explanation.surface: Police officers making an arrest and insisting on the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: Coppers could be coins, which suits 'deposit', but here they are police; copper is British slang for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means stating rules forcefully and insisting they be obeyed, being dogmatic about requirements.

clue.text: Fellow guzzling entire bottles

indicators.note: a bottle holds its contents inside, so the letters sit within the words

blocks.note: the last letter of one word and first three of the next

explanation.surface: A man drinking whole bottles, guzzling greedily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like a noun in a drinking scene, but it is a verb meaning holds. guzzlinG ENTire hides the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A gent is a gentleman, and fellow is an informal word for a man.

clue.text: One exceptionally good solver

blocks.note: first meaning: British informal praise for something excellent
second meaning: someone who breaks a code or solves a puzzle

explanation.walkthrough: The clue flatters the solver, but it is two meanings of one word. Calling a thing a cracker is British slang for saying it is excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Something outstanding is informally a cracker in Britain, and a codebreaker who cracks puzzles is also one.

clue.text: Break vacuous rule with venom

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so remove the inside and keep only the shell

blocks.note: the first and last letters
venom figuratively means malice or spite

explanation.surface: Someone flouts a pointless rule in a spiteful way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' looks like a verb about rule-breaking, but it is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A respite is a short rest or pause from something difficult, an interval of relief.

clue.text: Father fascinating woman endlessly

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: an alluring, dangerous woman

explanation.surface: A father endlessly fascinated by a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Sirens in myth lured sailors with song, so the word came to mean a seductive woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To sire is to beget offspring, and a sire is a male parent, especially of an animal.

clue.text: Uniting troubled council estates, leaving it with us worked

indicators.note: something troubled is disturbed and out of order
leaving means departing, so some letters go away
worked means shaped or kneaded, so the departing letters may come from anywhere in any order

blocks.note: the letters to work with
the letters to remove, wherever they fall

explanation.surface: A social project to bring together troubled housing estates, with us doing the work.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I, T, U and S from the fourteen letters and rearrange the ten left. A council estate is British public housing.
explanation.definitionFit: Coalescent means coming together to form one whole, merging, which is what uniting things do.
